newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt to sell shares in 20 firms in second half 97.
newsitem.headline: Egypt to sell shares in 20 firms in second half 97.

text.p: The minister in charge of Egyptian privatisation said on Wednesday he would bring shares in 20 state companies to the market in the second half of the year.

Public Enterprise Minister Atef Obeid told reporters that by the end of this month the government would have partially privatised 88 companies, up from 68 at the end of 1996. "By the end of the year it will be 108 (companies)," he added.
The minister did not name any of the companies and the target was slightly lower than the one he set at the start of the year -- 51 companies in all of 1997.
Brokers have learnt from experience to treat the government's privatisation forecasts with extreme caution, though the gap between promises and performance has been narrowing over the past 12 months.
The pace of privatisation, part of an economic reform programme which started in 1991, has increased rapidly since Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri took office in January 1996.

Obeid, whose ministry controls about 300 public-sector companies, said the government would pursue the search for strategic investors in some of the firms, despite the mixed results of this method of sale so far.
"It's not that easy (to attract strategic investors)," he said. "In some cases we succeeded, in some we failed."

"But we'll prepare the profiles of the companies, bring financial institutions and investment banks (and) give them three choices -- either 100 percent ownership, or minority interest and management with an option to buy later on, or a management contract and technical assistance in privatisation.
"So it will be a wide variety of options," he added.
The state has advertised for strategic investors in dozens of companies but only in about four cases have the negotiations ended in an outright sale to a majority shareholder.
In most other cases the state has sold tranches of shares through the stock exchange to individuals and institutions.
Obeid said he was also pressing ahead with sales of state companies in toto to company employees -- a strategy adopted successfully with land reclamation firms.
This is what he hopes to do with the rice milling companies which the state set up in the Nile Delta in the 1980s and which are now under stiff competition from the private sector.

"Those working in these small companies are very interested in buying, provided you do the financial restructuring before selling, and, to our surprise, they also asked for labour restructuring before sale," Obeid said.
"Fortunately they have plenty of land and we will sell it to pay for the financial restructuring," he added.
Obeid said the long-delayed privatisation of some big state companies, such as Aluminium Company of Egypt and Sugar and Integrated Industries Company, was still in his plans.
"They are finishing evaluation. As soon as that's complete, the shares will be offered," he said.
Obeid said back in mid-1995 that he would bring shares in the aluminium company, which runs the only smelter in the country, to the market within a matter of months.
The minister said he thought the state's big contracting companies, like Arab Contractors, would have to be broken up and streamlined before they qualified for privatisation.
